claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can be homogenized and stabilized as a single-phase BCC alloy at high temperature.
Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed primarily by the composition-dependent Gibbs free-energy difference between BCC and FCC phases.
The BCC–FCC phase boundary is set by ΔG_bcc-fcc.
At high temperature, entropy and a high ΔG_bcc-fcc stabilize the BCC state.
Cooling narrows or decreases ΔG_bcc-fcc in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
The cooling-induced decrease in ΔG_bcc-fcc creates a thermodynamic driving force for transformation from BCC toward FCC.
Transformation from BCC toward FCC requires sufficient atomic diffusion and rearrangement.
Rapid quenching suppresses diffusion and kinetically preserves metastable BCC.
Slow cooling or prolonged annealing permits diffusion-driven transformation toward FCC.
Slow-cooled or extended-annealed samples will have a larger FCC phase fraction than rapidly quenched samples.
A rapidly quenched sample is used as the baseline against which slow-cooled and isothermally annealed samples are compared.
The rapidly quenched baseline retains a metastable single-phase BCC microstructure.
The proposed mechanism operates in a temperature window where diffusion is active but BCC is not intrinsically stable.
Temperatures well above the transformation range favor BCC sufficiently to mask the BCC-to-FCC transformation.
At very low temperatures, sluggish diffusion prevents a noticeable phase change.
Transformation thresholds and kinetics can vary with composition and experimental conditions.

The hypothesis is falsified if slow cooling or annealing produces no statistically significant increase in FCC fraction relative to the quenched baseline, or if transformation onset fails to correlate with the predicted ΔG_bcc-fcc trend.

contradictions.description: The sign convention for ΔG_bcc-fcc is not defined. The mechanism says a high ΔG stabilizes BCC while a decreasing or narrowing ΔG drives transformation to FCC; without an explicitly stated sign change or free-energy ordering, these statements are thermodynamically ambiguous and potentially inconsistent.
